query:
Survey of the ether theory as motivation of Maxwell's equations

In all the modern textbooks on electromagnetism that I have seen, Maxwell’s equations are introduced in a rather poorly motivated way, in my opinion. It is often left unexplained how one goes from experimental facts to the equations. Sometimes the equations are simply postulated from the very beginning, and only afterward is it shown how they account for the experiments.

As far as I understand, this can be explained by the fact that Maxwell himself derived his equations under the assumption that the electromagnetic field represents a certain mechanical deformation of a hypothetical ether.

The ether theory was mainstream in 19th-century physics; both optics and electromagnetism were based on the assumption of its existence. Predictions of these theories agreed remarkably well with numerous experiments. However, the concept of the ether was abandoned following the Michelson-Morley experiment and the development of special relativity.

My impression is that once the ether was discarded, the original motivation for Maxwell’s equations largely disappeared.

I wonder if there exists a survey of the ether theory that provides a basic understanding of how Maxwell originally obtained his equations.
gold_answers: E. Whittaker, A history of the theories of aether and electricity, vol. 1. Harper and Bro. NY 1960 (third edition). Original edition, Thomas Nelson and Sons, 1910.

query:
Historical precedents for multiple independent theories converging on the same dimensionless constant before experimental confirmation?

In the history of science, there are cases where disparate theoretical frameworks predicted the same numerical value for a fundamental constant, sometimes years before precise measurements confirmed (or refuted) it. For example:

The Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) cutoff (~10^{20} eV) emerged from independent astrophysical arguments in the 1960s and was later observationally supported.

Conversely, early "derivations" of the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137 (e.g., Eddington's numerology) converged spuriously and were dismissed.

Planck's constant h appeared in blackbody radiation fits around 1900, with convergent estimates from thermodynamics and quantum hypotheses before full quantum mechanics.

What are other historical examples where ~3-5 independent derivations converged tightly (e.g., factor of 3-10) on a dimensionless (or scaled) constant prior to definitive experiments? How did scientists at the time interpret such convergences—as strong evidence for a new law, or potential coincidence?

I'm interested in: Cases from physics (e.g., cosmology's Λ wild divergences vs. convergences elsewhere), math (e.g., Khinchin's constant in continued fractions), or other fields.
What distinguished "meaningful" convergences (leading to laws like relativity's c) from numerological traps?
Any formalized historical debates on this epistemology (e.g., in Popper/Bayesian contexts)?

This stems from modern theories where rigidity theorems force functional forms, but magnitudes converge via independent routes (e.g., thermodynamic, holographic, statistical). References to papers/books on scientific prediction history welcome!

I'm researching how scientists historically distinguished between:

  • Meaningful convergence (e.g., multiple routes to c in relativity)
  • Numerological coincidence (e.g., Eddington's α theories)

What formal criteria emerged from these debates?
gold_answers:
Your question presupposes many wrong things. Even in the title

[...] multiple independent theories [...]

is just not the case. Scientific theories are not the theory as used colloquially. There might at most be multiple different arguments stemming from the same theory that leads to convergent values. If different scientific theories agree on a phenomenon, then usually the simpler theory is chosen to present the derivation, though of course, the deeper theory must also have a derivation of its own.

Your title also says that you want to focus upon

[...] dimensionless constant [...]

but your question body brings up the GZK cutoff, in units of eV, Planck's constant, which has units of action, cosmological constant, which has units of per area, and speed of light from Special Theory of Relativity $c$, which has units of length per time.

It is difficult to see how you could be understanding the very words that you are using.

It is also clear that you really just want us to do the work of finding other examples as stated in your question, so that you can cite them when trying to push your crackpottery. Sadly for you, you will not succeed, even if we do produce examples that you want.

But I want to make clear something that you are not appreciating at all. You speak of the Planck's constant as if it came alone. That is very much not the case.

Planck did not understand quantum theory even after having worked out his Planck's distribution law. The very early starting points before Planck came onto the scene was that there were Rayleigh–Jeans's Law and Wien's distribution law, and what Planck did was to first try to make the smallest change he could make to Wien's distribution law to make it agree with Rayleigh–Jeans's law, and found out that that made it work for all temperatures, and he published that first. Next, he worked very hard to try and give a theoretical justification for the new Planck's distribution law that he produced earlier. The theoretical justification is only sensible under quantum theory, but he made it clear what were necessary to get this correct result.

Planck's distribution law obviously used the Planck's constant $h$, but it did not come alone. In fact, there was no need for Planck's distribution law if all you wanted was to get those constants.

Since Rayleigh–Jeans's law works for the low energy part of the emission spectrum, simply just fitting the low energy part alone will extract $k_B$. The molar gas constant $R=N_Ak_B$ was known earlier, and that means that extracting $k_B$ also gives us Avogadro's constant $N_A$ for free.

Once you have $k_B$, Wien's distribution law, which works for the high energy portion of the spectrum, then gives us Planck's constant $h$.

What really happened, is that prior to Planck's properly theoretically justified derivation of his own distribution law, and then later Einstein's use of Planck's work to explain other mysteries, there was no good reason to expect that any of those constants are universal in application. They just appeared to be a big mass of glued-together constants that nobody knew the correct physical interpretation thereof. Because they were completely unidentified, there was no way to extract just the constant alone from any experimental measurement, and thus you can do all the experiments and numerology in the world, and there would be no use at all in making sense of the phenomena. This is why nobody was able to make the determination of $k_B$ from Rayleigh–Jeans's Law and determine $h$ from Wien's distribution law, and instead had to wait for Planck to get everything correct.

It is, however, remarkable that the pioneers working on the problem recognised the ultraviolet catastrophe before 1900.

Planck himself initially did not believe in his oscillation quanta. His proper theoretical derivation and justification pointed out that this $h$ quantum is necessary, but other than that little bit, he did not believe it had significance anywhere else.

What Einstein did was to push for this quantisation to be taken seriously, elevating it from an oddity to a general phenomenon. His annus mirabilis was a set of 4 papers, two on quantum theory and two on the Special Theory of Relativity.

The first paper was on the photoelectric effect, using Planck's constant. In this newly created theoretical answer to the effect, even though modern quantum theory itself would not be born for another 20 years, he asserted that there would be just this one single Planck's constant for the slope of a particular line.

This was not a theoretical idea that went without a fight. Robert Millikan, of finding the elementary charge $e$ fame (and in so doing, also $m_e$), was initially hating the idea. He spent ten years doing the photoelectric effect to ridiculous levels of precision and cleanliness, on both Lithium and Sodium, only to show that Einstein is correct that that particular slope is exactly the same Planck's constant, independent of the type of metal used for the photoelectric effect, exactly as Einstein predicted it.

Even after these successes, there were still plenty of argumentation, even after the proper formulation of the modern quantum mechanics, until the collective weight of the experimental evidence for quantum theory completely quelled academic dissent on the matter.

Indeed, Einstein himself became world famous from 1919 onwards, after Eddington publicly announced that Einstein's 1915 General Theory of Relativity was correct, overthrowing Newtonian flat space. Einstein was nominated as the sole recipient of the Nobel prize for relativity for two consecutive years, 1921 and 1922, and it was blocked by stupid bickering over a philosopher who really did not understand how spacetime could curve. The way out, was to just give it to him for photoelectric effect.

Einstein's other annus mirabilis paper about quantum theory was on the Brownian motion. That paper has a totally another method to find the pair $(k_B,N_A)$, and it also agrees with the one found from Planck's distribution law.

Note how it is necessary to be careful to distinguish between the properly formulated complete scientific theory, and the theoretical justifications and hypotheses and arguments made within them or along the way to a new one of them.

query:
Question about the history of the definition of the second in SI

This question is about specifically:

Why, in 1967, did the 13th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), choose 9192631770 cycles of radiation (corresponding to the transition between the two hyperfine levels of the ground state of the cesium-133 atom) to define a second and not a value that was perfect match to $\frac{1}{86400}$ solar day at that time?.

With that many cycles defining a second, at that time, circa 1965-1967, the mean solar day was about 2 or 2.5 ms longer than 86400 SI seconds. Why didn't they define the second to be 9192631982 cycles of this same cesium-133 radiation?

At what year (and I don't mean in the very recent past, but when atomic clocks were a new thing) was the mean solar day exactly 86400 SI seconds? What was the historical basis for the difference in the redefinition of a second to be consistent with the previous definition at that time?
gold_answers:
A good review addressing the question is:

  • Lombardi, M. A., Heavner, T. P., & Jefferts, S. R. (2007). NIST primary frequency standards and the realization of the SI second. NCSLI Measure, 2(4), 74-89.

Compare also the wikipedia entry on Ephemeris time.

The detailed story here is complicated, and there are numerous aspects of the question that do not directly map to the historical development. Specifically, the comparison of ephemeris time was not centered around 1967, but around 1957, and was not based on the mean solar day. It turns out that measuring the moon's motion is more precise than measuring the sun's.

The detailed measurements comparing Ephemeris Time with Cesium transition frequency was conducted and documented in:

  • Markowitz, W., Hall, R. G., Essen, L., & Parry, J. V. L. (1958). Frequency of cesium in terms of ephemeris time. Physical Review Letters, 1(3), 105.

1967 was not a hard transition from a mean solar day standard. Instead there was a transition period, considerations spanned the 1950's leading to a definition in 1960 of the second as:

the second is the fraction 1/31,556,985.974 7 of the tropical year for 1900 January 0 at 12 hours ephemeris time

Clearly the notion of mean day had already been replaced with a fixed period at a fixed date. This however should be seen as part of a transition towards an atomic clock-based norm.

Discussions of the standard committees were chronicled by Terrien. A longer form exposition of the period can be found in where the ultimate adoption of the 1967 is already strongly anticipated:

  • Terrien, J. (1965). Scientific metrology on the international plane and the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures. Metrologia, 1(1), 15.

Here we find an explanation for the transition to the 1960 definition:

The unit of time of the physicists, the second, has been defined as the fraction 1/86,400 of the mean solar day. Determination of the mean solar day is not a simple matter, but, again, atronomers [sic] could do it by observing the apparent angular movements of celestial bodies caused by the rotation of the Earth around its axis. But it was discovered that this rotation is slowing down, and, in addition, it varies in an erratic manner, as proved by observation of the Moon, or of Mercury, or, more recently, by comparison of astronomical time with quartz clocks. Astronomers then chose to define the second in terms of the year, instead of the day, that is to use as a standard the duration of one revolution of the Earth around the Sun, when numerous corrections have been applied. Even the duration of the year, the tropical year to be more precise, changes slowly by a known amount.

query:
What did people call a newton before 1948?

According to Wikipedia, the term newton, for the unit of force, was agreed in 1948.

However, both the metric system, as well as the idea of force as a physical concept, long predated this date.

Did people just write kg m/s$^2$ everywhere, or did they have some other name for this unit?
gold_answers:
The international system (meter-kilogram-second) with newton as the unit of force was proposed in 1948 and accepted in 1960. Before that there were two main metric systems:

CGS (centimeter-gram-second), where the unit of force was $\mathrm g\cdot \mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{sec}^2= \mathrm{dyne}$, and

"Gravitational system of units" (metre-Kilogram-second) where the Kilogram (force) was the unit of force, and kilogram (mass) was the unit of mass. Kilogram (force) was defined as the weight of one kilogram-mass at a specified place on Earth. This system was mostly used in engineering.

When I studied in high school (in Soviet Union) in 1960s the knowledge of all three systems was required :-)

query:
Historical description of electromagnetism as curvature

I have a vague memory of hearing somewhere that people had tried to describe electromagnetism as a curvature in space (not spacetime) prior to Einstein coming up with general relativity. However, when I try to search for this, I mostly find results about the Kaluza-Klein theory after relativity.

Is this a false memory, or is there some paper written prior to general relativity attempting to describe electromagnetism as a curvature in space?
gold_answers:
As pointed out in the comments, you may be looking for the works of Gunnar Nordström. His 1913 theory of gravitation was the first metric theory of gravitation, but it did not obey the equivalence principle. In 1914-1915 he published three papers introducing a five-dimensional theory aiming to unify electromagnetism and gravitation.

However, I would not call that theory a description of electromagnetism "as a curvature in space (not spacetime)". Rather, Nordström argued that the physical spacetime can be viewed as a hypersurface of a five-dimensional space, where one of the five coordinates retains its connection to physical time. To quote a description of the first 1914 paper by Frank Borg,

This is the first paper by Gunnar Nordström (1881-1923) on his five dimensional theory. In his summary he states: "It is shown, that a unifying treatment of the electromagnetic and gravitational fields is possible, if one considers the four dimensional spacetime world to be a surface in a five dimensional world." This paper was followed by two other papers written by Gunnar Nordström during the one year period 1914-1915, on the same subject, which are also made available here. What Nordström called "Welt-fläche" (world-surface) is nowadays termed a brane. Nordström's theory was thus a precursor of the modern brane- and 5D-theories. His basic idea was to unify electromagnetism and gravitation (in the form of Nordström's scalar theory) by extending the basic formalism of Maxwell's electromagnetic theory, as developed by Minkowski, to a five dimensional space of which physical space-time is a hypersurface. Modern 5D-theories use the same basic approach but start instead from Einstein's general theory of relativity which is extended to the 5D-case. Einstein's theory was of course only in its final gestation when Nordström worked on his theory, and the full impact of geometry on physics was only to become apparent later. Subsequently Theodor Kaluza (1921) and Oskar Klein (1926) also seized on the idea of spacetime extension as a path toward unification. - F.B.

The three relevant papers are

  • G. Nordström: "Über die Möglichkeit, das elektromagnetische Feld und das Gravitationsfeld zu vereinigen." [On the possibility of unifying the electromagnetic and the gravitational fields]. Physik. Zeitschr. XV (1914) p. 504-506. [English translation by F. Borg available at arXiv:physics/0702221].
  • G. Nordström: "Zur Elektricitäts- und Gravitationstheorie" [On a theory of electricity and gravitation]. Översigt af Finska Vetenskaps-Societetens Förhandlingar (Helsingfors), Bd. LVI I. 1914-1915. Afd. A. N:o 4, p. 1-15. [English translation by F. Borg available at arXiv:physics/0702222].
  • G. Nordström: "Über eine mögliche Grundlage einer Theorie der Materie" [On a possible foundation of a theory of matter]. Översigt av Finska Vetenskaps-Societetens Förhandlingar Bd. LVII. 1914-1915. Afd. A. N:o 28, p. 1-21. [English translation by F. Borg available at arXiv:physics/0702223].

Frank Borg made the original papers (in German) available here and prepared the English translations linked above.

query:
How did mathematicians justify using imaginary numbers before complex analysis made them rigorous?

In the 16th and 17th centuries, some mathematicians solved cubic equations using what we now call imaginary numbers, long before the concept of the complex plane. How did they justify using $\text{“}\sqrt{-1}\text{”}$ when it didn’t have a defined meaning yet, and what arguments eventually convinced mathematicians that it was legitimate to use such quantities?
gold_answers:
In the case of cubic and other equations, the use of complex numbers was justified by the results obtained. Once you obtain a real root of an equation by manipulating with complex numbers, you can then verify directly (or convince yourself by approximate computation) that this is indeed a root.

Similar situations are abundant in mathematics. For example, modern physicists (and engineers) use mathematically unjustified methods to obtain results which then can be checked by either rigorous methods or by experiments. Some examples are 1. Use of Fourier series by Fourier (and people before him) 2. Use of distributions in Heaviside's "operational calculus", 3. Use of unbounded operators in quantum mechanics before von Neumann defined them, 4. Many results obtained by modern physicists using "quantum field theory", 5. Feynman's "integral over paths", etc.

In all these examples, a mathematical object was effectively used long before its rigorous justification, and even before its rigorous definition.

Returning to numbers, real numbers were used at least from 17 century, or much earlier. But the rigorous definition was given only in the end of 19 century.

query:
Origin of ramification/inertia in number theory?

I'm self-studying algebraic number theory, currently going over ramification. How primes split in extensions, and the nomenclature seem fine to me. In my notes I like to keep some historical references when I'm able to, but I'm struggling with these particular subject, as I haven't been able to identify them.

I've read essentially that (1) Hilbert was behind all of ramification, or that (2) he compiled what was known of ramification and he contributed with higher ramification (in the Galois case). Both statements poorly backed if by any source at all (for an example see the Wikipedia page).

So, my question is double: what was Hilbert's actual contribution to ramification, and if he is not the original author of the idea, then how it came to be?

I've read upon Hilbert's Zahlbericht and he does not state his ideas are original, nor if he got them from somewhere else. Also I've checked the 1894 version of Dedekind–Dirichlet's Vorlesungen hoping that the original ideas on ramification just weren't translated, but that wasn't helpful either.

Thanks in advance.
gold_answers:
The higher ramification groups are definitely due to Hilbert. They appeared in 1894 here (see p. 231 in the full text link), which is a webpage that unfortunately misspells the name as D. Hubert. I wrote to eudml.org months ago about this error but never heard back.

Anyway, ramification as a general phenomenon in algebraic number theory was recognized before Hilbert. There was an influential paper by Dedekind and Weber in 1882 called "Theory of Algebraic Functions of One Variable" that developed the theory of Riemann surfaces (really, function fields) purely algebraically so that it made sense with a constant field that is the field of algebraic numbers rather than the complex numbers, or more generally, from a modern point of view, with a constant field that could be any algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$.

The inspiration for the Dedekind--Weber paper was to apply methods of algebraic number theory to the geometric setting of function fields. The original paper by Dedekind and Weber is here. A translation into English is in a book by Stillwell here. Hilbert was not involved with any of this: in 1882 he was still an undergraduate at Koenigsberg. A paper from 2017 by Haffner that discusses Dedekind and Weber's work is here, and it mentions that Weber saw analogies between the different ideal and discriminant of a number field and the ramification points on a Riemann surface. In a footnote on page 56, Haffner writes

Dedekind, in [Dedekind, 1882], transferred the ramification ideal (renamed Grundideal, fundamental ideal) back to number theory.

The paper mentioned there by Dedekind from 1882 is where he introduced the discriminant and different ideal of a number field. Hilbert later renamed the Grundideal as the different ideal in his Zahlbericht.

In short, ramification arose first in the study of Riemann surfaces and later this terminology was brought into algebraic number theory.

query:
How long did it take the physics community to accept J. J. Thomson's electron theory?

How long did it take the physics community to accept J. J. Thomson's electron theory?

For example, the anti-atomist Pierre Duhem (d. 1916) never commented on it.

There are books written on the reception of relativity theory (e.g., Glick, The Comparative Reception of Relativity), but are there are ones written on the acceptance of the electron theory?
gold_answers:
The problem with this type of questions is that there is no clear answer. Scientific consensus does not have a specific date. Clearly people close to Thomson accepted it faster than people far away. Also people like Pierre Duhem, Ernst Mach or Wilhelm Ostwald were anti-atomists so they were biased and did not believe in electrons or any kind atomistic composition. Duhem never acknoledged anything related to Einstein anyway (not even Brownian motion that allowed to confirm the existence of atoms).

One key event that allowed Thomson theory to get better established was the International Congress of Physics during the 1900 Universal Exposition in Paris. It is said that French physicists were still skeptical of the electron and came up with all kinds of alternatives. However, not only did the congress allow for the electrons to get more ground in France and Europe, but also Paul Drude showed in the same congress that he could explain properties of metals using electrons (Drude model). The Curie's were also supportive of the electron hypothesis to explain certain radioactive phenomena. The Dutch and German physicists had no problem with the electron.

So already three years after the discovery of the electron, it was recognized internationally by major physicists, and people were explaining other phenomena with it. And if this was not enough, 6 years later Thomson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Paul U. Villard (the discoverer of γ-rays), who was the main opponent of Thomson in France, accepted Thomson's hypothesis in 1908 (see (1)). Interestingly, the same year Ostwald accepted the existence of atoms.

There is an extra interesting point in (1). J.J. Thomson did not want to use the word "electron"; he preferred the word corpuscle, and did not use the word "electron" until 1913.

References:

  1. B. Lelong, Paul Villard, J.-J. Thomson et la composition des rayons cathodiques, Revue d'histoire des sciences (1997) 50-1-2 pp. 89-130 (in French)

For the International Congress of Physics you can check:

  • H. Kragh, Quantum Generations: A History of Physics in the Twentieth Century
  • S. Richard, Einstein's Generation: The Origins of the Relativity Revolution University of Chicago Press.

For the challenges with the atomists vs anti-atomists, maybe:

  • D. Lindley, Boltzmann's atom, Simon & Schuster

query:
Where does "Gödel numbers" come from?

Confer my question "First use of corner quotes for Gödel numbers" crossposted to
History of Science and Mathematics, https://hsm.stackexchange.com/questions/14817/first-use-of-corner-quotes-for-gödel-numbers, and Mathoverflow, https://mathoverflow.net/questions/430869/first-use-of-corner-quotes-for-gödel-numbers/431347?_gl=1*1g050n1*_ga*OTQxOTU4NTg5LjE3NTUwMzEzMDA.*_ga_S812YQPLT2*czE3NTU5NjgyMTkkbzQ1JGcxJHQxNzU1OTY4MjQyJGozNyRsMCRoMA..#431347.

The Mathoverflow posting obtained the answer that Georg Kreisel used corner quotes for Gödel numbers in the abstracts: The subformula property and reflection principles, JSL 28(4):305-306, 1963; Reflection principle for Heyting's arithmetic, JSL 28(4):306-307, 1963 & Reflection principles and 𝜔-consistency, JSL 28(4):307-8, 1963.

Wikipedia on Gödel numbering states: "Since the publishing of Gödel's paper in 1931, the term "Gödel numbering" or "Gödel code" has been used to refer to more general assignments of natural numbers to mathematical objects."

But Gödel did not use the term "Gödel-number". Nor did Quine, who introduced the corner quotes $\ulcorner \ \urcorner$ in the 1st edition of Mathematical Logic (and retained in the Revised Edition of 1950), without relating them to Gödel numbers, however. Nevertheless, Kreisel must after all have been inspired by Quine, I think, especially given the latter's deep boring:

@article{Quine1946, author = {Quine, W.~V.}, ISSN = {00224812}, URL = {http://www.jstor.org/stable/2268308}, journal = {The Journal of Symbolic Logic}, number = {4}, pages = {105--114}, publisher = {Association for Symbolic Logic}, title = {Concatenation as a Basis for Arithmetic}, urldate = {2025-08-19}, volume = {11}, year = {1946} }.

My question is: Who coined the term "Gödel number"?

Update on August 24, 2025: Communication with Mauro Allegranza in the comments section revealed that @book{NagelNewman1958, author = {Nagel, E. and Newman, J.~R.}, publisher = {New York University Press}, title = {Godel's Proof}, year = {1958} } uses "Gödel number".
gold_answers:
A good starting point will be Stephen Cole Kleene, Introduction to Metamathematics (1952), both for the prestige and for the date of first printing: 1952.

See page 206:

We call this a Gödel numbering, and the correlated number of a formal object its Gödel number.

Following this track, we can go back to Stephen Cole Kleene, Recursive predicates and quantifiers (1943), page 47:

For a suitably chosen Gödel numbering, we can show [...] with $f$ as the Gödel number of the system of equations $F$.

See also Stephen Cole Kleene, On the interpretation of intuitionistic number theory (JSL, 1945), page 113: "The formula $(\forall x)A(x)$ is realized by the Gödel number $e$ of a general recursive function $\phi$ such that..."

Early on we have Alonzo Church, An Unsolvable Problem of Elementary Number Theory (Am.Jou.of Mathematics, 1936) that does not use the term; see page 349: "The Gödel representation of a formula. Adapting to the formal notation just described a device which is due to Gödel, we associate with every formula a positive integer to represent it, as follows [...] This number will be called the Gödel representation of the formula..."

Next we have Alan Turing, On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem (Proc.London Math.Soc, 1936), page 248: "$G(n)$ might mean '$n$ is the Gödel representation of a provable formula' ."

Thus we arrive at Haskell Curry, The Paradox of Kleene and Rosser (1941), page 467:

The Gödel representation. [... page 469] which enumerates the Gödel numbers of those assertions.

And finally, we arrive at the [I think] source: J.Barkley Rosser, Extensions of Some Theorems of Gödel and Church (JSL, 1936), page 87:

By an "Entscheidungsverfahren" will be meant a general recursive function $\phi(n)$ such that, if $n$ is the Gödel number [emphasis added] of a provable formula, $\phi(n) = 0$ and, if $n$ is not the Gödel number of a provable formula, $\phi(n) = 1$.

query:
How influential was Claude Shannon in the 50s and 60s?

I have been attempting to study cryptography as a time-line, from the beginning. I have lazily studied until 1949's publication of Claude Shannon's work which funded modern cryptography. I have mostly seen non-mathematical ciphers and cipher machines, which mostly seem to be about being as complex and clever as possible. Neither of these felt modern in relation to Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange, but Shannon's work did — and interestingly so did OTP, and I expected a similar feeling in the 50s. However, as I went to study the 50s... everything I saw seemed mostly an evolution of the old, nothing felt modern or truly mathematical like Claude Shannon. And I couldn't find evolutions of theoretical cryptography.

This was similar in the 60s, but in the 70s, everything was different: Lucipher, Diffin-Hellman, DES. Then, stuff felt "modern" again.

What happened?! Why does it seem like there is almost a void of advancements since Claude Shannon and OTP in (what feels like) modern cryptography?

A guess.

Interestingly, when I went to Wikipedia's page "History of Cryptography", I saw the following quote.

Until the 1960s, secure cryptography was largely the preserve of governments. Two events have since brought it squarely into the public domain: the creation of a public encryption standard (DES), and the invention of public-key cryptography.

This leads me to guess two things: 1) the need for secure system in non-governmental spaces, was not that high and of different nature, and 2) the need for secure systems in non-governmental that existed was well served with OTP, rotor ciphers and those telegram cipher machines. And I guess that in the late 60s and 70s, the IC revolution with the high availability of microcomputers and growing interest in computers networks, made the need grow for better and different cryptography.
gold_answers:
This is not an answer, rather some contextual points to consider that are rough and somewhat speculative:

  • Post World-War 2 effects. Mathematicians in many countries were participating in encryption and code breaking efforts, but returned to non-war interests after the war.
  • National Security interests. Even Shannon's 1949 paper was delayed 4 years due to the need to the material becoming declassified it was written in 1945 and reflected Shannon's wartime interest in the topic. Exploring the evolution of national security institutions may help clarify non-public developments. E.g. the NSA in the US was founded in 1952. See also more about the reaction of the NSA to Diffie-Hellman.
  • Technological developments. Specialized hardware as normative in the 1940s and general purpose computation was just emerging. The field would transition towards software-based cryptography with the the maturing and availability of general purpose computing that is no longer isolated. Diffie-Hellman would open with recognizing the hardware evolution as follows: "We stand today on the brink of a revolution in cryptography. The development of cheap digital hardware has freed it [..]"
  • Theoretical advances. Emergence of complexity theory allows the study of the difficulty of a problem. Complexity theory emerged from the mid 1950s to mature through the 1960s. It is instructive to look at the references cited in Diffie-Hellmen to recognize the impact matured theory of algorithms and complexity had on their work. Such aspects tend to be overlooked because they are not cryptography itself but enabling developments.

query:
How were Maxwell's works on electrodynamics received by his contemporaries?

In a recent answer to a question on this site, the claim was made that

Maxwell's works were incomprehensible because Maxwell is incredibly sloppy about units and kept rewriting his own equations, constants of proportionality kept migrating from numerator to denominator and vice versa.

And further in a comment,

None of the contemporaries could understand Maxwell, but they could understand Heaviside, and so Heaviside became the one to introduce Maxwellian electrodynamics to the world.

The scope of these comments was relating to electromagnetics, and in particular the permittivity $\epsilon$ and permeability $\mu$.

Are these statements generally applicable to Maxwell, both in his historical context and/or in retrospect? Specifically:

  • Were Maxwell's works considered "incomprehensible" by his contemporaries because of his sloppiness with units?
  • Did Maxwell himself "introduce Maxwellian electrodynamics to the world" or was his work mostly promoted through Heaviside?
gold_answers:
Here's a quote from the historical introduction of Sommerfeld's electrodynamics (1952). He begins with the situation leading up to Maxwell's Treatise which he describes as "difficult":

My time of study coincided with the period of Hertz’s experiments. At first, however, electrodynamics was still presented to us in the old manner - in addition to Coulomb and Biot-Savart, Ampere's law of the mutual action of two elements of currents and its competitors, the laws of Grassmann, Gauss, Riemann, and Clausius, and as a culmination the law of Wilhelm Weber, all of which were based on the Newtonian concept of action at a distance. The total picture of electrodynamics thus presented to us was awkward, incoherent, and by no means self-contained. Teachers and students made a great effort to familiarise themselves with Hertz's experiments step by step as they became known and to explain them with the aid of the difficult original presentation$^1$ in Maxwell's Treatise.

He then sings the praise of Hertz's theoretical contributions (mentioning Heaviside briefly):

It was as though scales fell from my eyes when I read Hertz's great paper$^2$: "Über die Grundgleichungen der Elektrodynamik für ruhende Körper”. Here Maxwell's equations, purified by Heaviside and Hertz, were made the axioms and the starting point of the theory. The totality of electromagnetic phenomena is derived from them systematically by deduction. Coulomb's law, which formerly provided the basis, now appears as a necessary consequence of the all-inclusive theory. Electric currents are always closed. Current elements arise only as mathematical increments of line integrals. All effects are transmitted by the electromagnetic field, which may be represented by force-line models. Action at a distance gives way to field action$^3$, the "constructable representation" of a space-time propagation postulated already by Gauss$^4$. I have held to the order of Hertz's paper in all my lectures on Maxwell's theory. In this presentation, too, we shall not begin with electrostatics, as is done so commonly and also in Maxwell's Treatise, but treat it merely as an extreme simplification of the general field theory. We shall deviate from Hertz only insofar as we shall start not from Maxwell's equations in differential form, but in integral form...

Footnotes:

  1. The great student of electrolysis, Wilhelm Hittorf, who had heard much of the new theory of electricity, in advanced years attempted to study the Treatise, but was unable to find his way through the unfamiliar mass of equations and concepts. He was thus led into a state of deep depression. His colleagues in Münster persuaded him to take a vacation trip to the Harz Mountains. However when just before his departure they checked his luggage they found in it - the two volumes of the Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism by James Clerk Maxwell. (As told by A. Heidweiller.)
  1. Göttinger Nachr. March 1890 and Ann. Physik, Vol. 40; continued in Ann. Physik, Vol. 41: “Über die Grundgleichungen der Elektrodynamik für bewegte Körper."
  1. We avoid the alternative term "near action" which signifies merely action at a small distance, and by our notation direct attention to the medium transmitting the effect, namely the field.
  1. In a letter to Wilhelm Weber, of 1845. See Collected Works, Vol. V, p. 627.

Footnote 1 is particularly illustrative...

query:
When did astrology pass out of medicine?

From the General Prologue of the Canterbury Tales, a 14th century collection of narrative poems:

With us ther was a Doctour of Phisik;

In all this world ne was ther noon hym lik,

To speke of phisik and of surgerye;

For he was grounded in astronomye.

He kepte his pacient a ful greet deel

In houres, by his magyk natureel.

Wel koude he fortunen the ascendent

Of his ymáges for his pacient.

He knew the cause of everich maladye,

Were it of hoot, or cold, or moyste, or drye,

And where they engendred and of what humour.

He was a verray, parfit praktisour;

In the above poem, we are introduced to the author's image of an ideal 14th century MD ("a very perfect practitioner"). He clearly practices humorism ("hot, or cold, or moist, or dry") as was typical at least up to the 17th century. I also note his use of astrological practices - he is "grounded in astronomy" and can "fortune the ascendant of his images for his patient".

My question is, at what point did astrology pass out of medical best practices or otherwise get discarded to the dustbin of medicine? Was it at the same time as the passing of humorism or at a different time?
gold_answers:
It is widely recognized that astronomical medicine was over at the (end of the) 17th century near the arrival of the Enlightenment in the sciences, but the exact date is unclear, as explained here

  • H. G. Dick, "A SURVEY OF ASTROLOGICAL MEDICINE IN THE AGE OF SCIENCE" Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, 1 (1946) pp. 300-315 (part 2 here)

Robert Burton writes in 1621:

Astrology is required by many famous Physicians, by Ficinus, Crato, Fernelius, doubted of and exploded by others. I will not take upon me to decide the controversy myself; Johannes Hossurtus, Thomas Boderius, and Maginus in the Preface to his Mathematical Physick, shall determine for me. Many Physicians explode Astrology in Physick, (saith he), there is no use of it, an ill-advised art followed by those ignorant ones who are on the look-out for fame, but I will reprove Physicians by Physicians that defend and profess it, Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, &c., that count them butchers without it.

indicating that the conflict between science and astrology was developing.

In the English world, the last "accepted" astrological treatises (mid 17th century) came from William Lilly, Nicholas Culpeper and John Heydon. Dick cites the works of John Cotta and Charles Goodall against quack doctors and astrologers as a key events that led to the decline of medical astrology. See also John Gadbury who followed Lilly but then turned against him and denounced false practices in medical schools. Dick also considers the famous clash between the writer Jonathan Swift and John Partridge (1705) as an event that shaped the popular view on the matter.

Before that you still have astrology being central in Elizabethan medicine (1550-1603) as explained here:

  • C. Camdem Jr, "Elizabethan Astrological Medicine", Ann Med Hist. (1930) 2:217–226.

Humorism seems to have declined around the same time but the ultimate alternative came in the 19th century, credited to Rudolf Virchow's cellular pathology.

(I have no previous knowledge on this, I just read Wikipedia medical astrology's sources.)

Of course the banishing of medical astrology depended on the part of the world. In the Spanish speaking world (Spain and the Hispanic Americas), the use of astrological medicine was widespread in the 17th century, see:

  • T. M.C. Lanuza Navarro MedicaI Astrology in Spain During the Seventeenth Century* (2006)

query:
In what document was the expression "differential equation" first used?

Without providing a source, Ince's book (1920) claims that the expression aequatio differentialis (differential equation) was first used by Leibniz in 1676. This information is repeated in many other works.

The earliest record I have found of this expression appears in Leibniz’s Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis, dated 1684. Since this was the first publication in the history of Differential Calculus, Ince’s mention must refer to some letter.

Question: In which manuscript did Leibniz first use the expression aequatio differentialis?
gold_answers:
The first occurrence I could find is actually from November 1676 in Calculus tangentium differentialis:

Ut ista tractari possint ubi $d\bar{x}^2$, vel $d\bar{y}^2$ et similia, ut $d\bar{x}d\bar{y}$, quoniam illa ex simplici inventione differentiarum duci non possunt, fieri possunt variae aequationes simplices differentiales [emphasis mine], eaeque multiplicatae per $d\bar{x}$ vel $d\bar{y}$ aut eorum potentias componi inter se ad inveniendas aequationes novas.

i.e.

To deal also with cases where $d\bar{x}$, or $d\bar{y}$ and the like, such as $d\bar{x}d\bar{y}$, cannot be derived from the simple discovery of differences, some simple differential equations can be written, and these, then multiplied by $d\bar{x}$ or $d\bar{y}$ or their powers, can be combined to find new equations.

This work can be found in Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz: Sämtliche Schriften und Briefe, Mathematical Writings, Fifth volume: 1674-1676: Infinitesimal Mathematics; Edited by Uwe Mayer, Siegmund Probst, and Heike Sefrin-Weis (2008), p. 616.

query:
Examples of recordings of the transit of Venus before the 17th century?

Looking for the history of the observations of the transit of Venus, it seems that the first formal observation was in 1639 by Horrocks and Crabtree. However this observation happens during the times of Kepler and Galileo. Kepler apparently predicted both the first modern observations of the transit of both Venus and Mercury. Was it possible for somebody to record the transit of Venus before that time?

In the geocentric model of Ptolemy, the celestial sphere of Venus is closer to Earth than the sphere of the Sun, so at some point the transit has to happen. Wikipedia's article on the transit of Venus suggests that Avicenna might have observed the transit, but the article cast doubts about that possibility. Is there no other record of the transit let's say between between Pythagoras and Horrocks & Crabtree? How was it determined that Mercury and Venus were in the inner circles?
gold_answers:
For old records that could possibly show that an ancient or medieval astronomer observed a transit of Venus or Mercury over the sun's disk, a recommendable modern study is that by Bernard R Goldstein: "Some Medieval Reports of Venus and Mercury Transits", in Centaurus (1969) 14(1) pp.49—59. Exhaustive coverage would of course be impossible, and Goldstein understandably did not claim it. The records that he found included several mentions of phenomena that at first sight (of the record) could have referred to a transit of either Mercury or Venus.

All but one of the reports examined by Goldstein contained factors that would exclude that what was seen was a transit. Where there seemed to be enough information for a date to be ascertained, the date was far from the date of any transit (now known by retrospective modern calculation). Some of the records reported that the phenomenon had lasted for many days: but a transit only lasts a few hours at most.

(For example: The oldest report for which Goldstein cites (indirect) witness is an observation dated Tuesday, 19 Rajab 225 [equiv May 27, 840] made by al-Kindi, indirectly reported by al-Qifti and Averroes. The phenomenon, though, was said to last 91 days, and on the stated date Venus was actually near greatest elongation from the sun. Thus, two factors exclude that the al-Kindi observation was of a transit.)

To cut a long story short, Goldstein's conclusion was that

"It is clear that we do not have a well authenticated medieval report of a transit; the only report for which the observation of a transit cannot be excluded immediately is that of Avicenna, whose report includes too little information."

Unfortunately the conclusion 'too little information' also seems to apply equally to suggestive traces from Asia or meso-America.

If any earlier material is found, then its credibility (in the absence of issues such as forgery) would usually fall to be assessed by whatever its content turns out to be.

In general, there was risk of making confusion between a transiting planet and a sunspot. By the time of the 1639 Horrocks Venus transit observation (based on his own prediction) sunspots had been identified as such, and Horrocks's account takes care to offer clear reasons why his observation was different and not a sunspot. But sunspots were not known as such in more ancient times, hence a general risk of confusion.

query:
Square root defined as a positive value: why?, when? who?

In the Mathematics Educators Stack Exchange, a poster asked whether $\sqrt 4$ could be considered as both $+2$ and $-2$. However, in modern mathematics, $\sqrt 4$ is conventionally defined as $+2$. I thought that exploring the history of mathematics could help answer their question: who decided to choose the positive value as the standard definition of the square root, when did this convention become established, and why was this choice made?

This might seem like a naive question, but it's actually quite common among students and those learning mathematics.
gold_answers:
This answer only provides a rough outline, as I do not possess comprehensive knowledge of the history of European mathematics, let alone the global history of mathematics. The gist of the development process seems to have been be that square roots were exclusively positive for three millenia, then the square root began to be considered as a multi-valued operation for several centuries, until we mostly focused back on the principal branch at some time during the 20th century.

The Babylonian clay tablet YBC 7289 dated to about 1700 B.C. provides the first known evidence of a square root computation, giving $\sqrt{2}$ to three sexagesimal places: $1;24,51,10$. The exact process by which this result was computed is not known. The Greeks likely learned of square roots from the Babylonians. Hippasus of Metapontum (5th century B.C.) is credited with proving that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. Book X of Euclid's Elements (3rd century B.C.) demonstrates how to manipulate expressions involving square roots, although on a purely geometric basis. In the 1st century A.D. Heron of Alexandria gave a numerical method for computing square roots, likely of much older origin. Up to this point there was no notion of negative numbers in mathematics, thus all square roots were positive by default.

The Chinese book The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art from the 1st century A.D. contains the first known appearance of negative numbers, a concept further developed by the Chinese mathematician Liu Hui in the 3rd century. But it would be a long time before the concept was introduced into European mathematics. The 15th century French mathematician Nicholas Chuquet is credited with the first use of negative numbers, limited to exponents only [4].

From what I could find, Simon Stevin's L'Arithmetique (1585), contains the first examples of negative roots in the history of European mathematics, in the context of quadratic equations. One example is found in article II on p. 333, where he shows that $x^{2}=4x+21$ has a solution $-3$. The first direct presentation of the square root as a multi-valued operation that I could locate is in Colin MacLaurin's A Treatise of Algebra, published posthumously in 1748. On p. 43:

It appears from what was said of Involution, that "any Power that has a positive Sign may have either a positive or negative Root, if the Root is denominated by any even Number." Thus the square Root of $+a^{2}$ may be $+a$ or $−a$, because $+a \times +a$ or $−a \times −a$ gives $+a^{2}$ for the Product.

It should be noted that Indian mathematics had reached the equivalent notion by the 12th century. Henry Thomas Colebrooke (tr.), Algebra, with Arithmetic and mensuration, from the Sanscrit of Brahmegupta and Bháscara. London: John Murray 1817, p. 135 quotes from the Bījagaṇita (Algebra) of Bhāskara II (c. 1114-1185) as follows:

The square of an affirmative or of a negative quantity is affirmative; and the root of an affirmative quantity is two-fold, positive and negative. There is no square-root of a negative quantity: for it is not a square.

I was able to trace the presentation of the square root as a multi-valued operation through German textbooks [1,2,3] from 1768 right to the end of the 19th century, which suggests that this was a commonly and consistently held notion. J. Brunotte, Lehrbuch der Arithmetik und Algebra für Gymnasien, Real- und Handelsschulen. Nürnberg 1894, p. 78:

Da sowohl $(+a)^{2}=a^{2}$ als auch $(-a)^{2}=a^{2}$, so folgt $$\sqrt{a^2}=\begin{cases} +a \\ -a \end{cases} \ \ \text{ ebenso } \sqrt{4}=\begin{cases} +2 \\ -2 \end{cases} \ \ \ \ \sqrt{\frac{64a^{4}}{49x^{2}}} = \pm \frac{8a^{2}}{7x} $$

d.h. jede Quadratwurzel gibt zwei, nur dem Vorzeichen nach entgegengesetzte Werte, ist also im allgemeinen zweideutig. In den folgenden Untersuchungen und Rechnungen werden jedoch nur die absoluten Werte in Betracht gezogen werden.

This notes that the square root operation is multi-valued, but advises the reader that the further text will consider the absolute values only.

Google Books does not constitute a good source for literature past the 1920s, presumably due to copyright issues, so I have had no luck in tracing the presentation of the square root in textbooks for middle schools or high schools any further. I do not recall what happened in my own math classes, but located among my books one widely used mathematical textbook from Germany (Lambacher-Schweizer) from 1981, where the "Quadratwurzelfunktion" (square root function) is defined as $\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+} \mapsto \mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}$, that is, covering the principal branch only.

Some commenters under this question have opined that the focus back on the principal branch was a consequence of the introduction of electronic calculators and programming languages for computers (in particular since about 1970) whose $\sqrt{}$ keys and sqrt() math library functions are limited to that. I consider that plausible, but not conclusive evidence.

[1] Heinrich Wilhelm Klemm, Mathematisches Lehrbuch. Stuttgart 1768, p. 127: "Eine jede quadratische Gleichung hat 2 Wurzeln, dann von $x^{2}$ kann $+x$ und $−x$ die Wurzel seyn."

[2] Joseph Melchior Danzer, Mathematisches Lehrbuch. Erster Teil. Munich 1781, p. 66: "Alle Wurzeln von geraden Exponenten können also zweyerley seyn, positiv und negativ. $\sqrt{9}=\pm 3$. Die Wurzeln von ungeraden Exponenten aber haben nur das Zeichen, welches ihre Würde hat. Z.B. $\sqrt[3]{−8}=−2$."

[3] Franz Minsinger, Lehrbuch der Arithmetic und Algebra. Augsburg 1832, p. 100: "Das Ausziehen der Quadratwurzel aus Zahlen (ganzen, gemischten und gebrochenen) ist bekanntlich das Zerfällen der gegebenen Zahlen in zwei gleiche Faktoren, daher die gegebene Zahl stets positiv sein muß, die Wurzel aber positiv und negativ sein kann. [...] z.B. $\sqrt{81}=\pm 9$

[4] Chuquet used $\bar{\mathrm{p}}.$ for $+$ and $\bar{\mathrm{m}}.$ for $-$. One of his examples is the multiplication of $8^{3}$ by $7^{1 \bar{\mathrm{m}}.}$ resulting in $56^{2}$, meaning (I think) $8x^{3} \cdot 7x^{-1} = 56x^{2}$.

query:
Who discovered that vacuum tubes could be used for logic and computation?

When I search of the origin of vacuum tubes or even look up how they work, their usage as amplifiers is stressed, but their usage as logic devices is seldom mentioned. When I look up the background of the main engineers working on the early computing machines with vacuum tubes (ABC, ENIAC, Colossus), I do not see anything connecting them except knowing electronics. Further, the ABC was apparently not well known, and Colossus was a secret until the 70s. I am excluding their use for memory, since the "Eccles–Jordan Trigger Circuit" was already known and apparently used in radars.

What was the first time people knew that vacuum tubes could be used for logic and computation?

I have two guesses. The first one is that it was obvious, because people knew that vacuum tubes could be used as switches and knew of Claude Shannon's master thesis.

The second guess is that it was rediscovered 3 times independently. First, the Colossus engineers discovered it, but kept it secret. Second, by the ABC engineers, but their invention was not widely known, nor they seemed to have an interest in such press or research. Then, the ENIAC engineers discovered it a third time and this knowledge was shared by the ENIAC's team, most importantly through the Moore School Lectures. However, if this theory were correct, then wouldn't the fact that the ENIAC engineers discovered this property of vacuum tubes be widely mentioned?
gold_answers:
The historical context was the needs of telegraphy and then telephony, as important technological advances allowing long range communication.

This, in some sense, is an independent precursor to computers from the traditional history of computing machinery.

A good overview of the development of computing is:

  • Copeland, B. Jack, (2000/2006) "The Modern History of Computing", The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Edward N. Zalta (ed.).

For our purpose it is relevant that the innovation of the vacuum tube was the speed of switching, not that one can switch. Electromechanical computing already understood that concept.

That vacuum tubes could switch was understood due to the needs of wireless telegraphy and other forms of communication circuitry (via for example pulse-code modulation and related multiplexing circuitry that were used as early as 1853 by Farmer). While vacuum tube amplification use was important, it was well known that their properties could be used in various ways, including detection, modulation, and wave shaping.

Shannon's work itself actually talks about connectivity states as related to logical 0/1 states, compare this discussion, hence in this sense bridges the analog but idealized switching level with a more abstracted digital (logical) level. Actually building a computer still needs to consider the analog nature, and make sure that there is a proper "digital" (stable) operation to allow the logic to work as intended "abstractly".

Here is how Shannon motivated his thesis (p.1) from application realms:

In the control and protective circuits of complex electrical systems it is frequently necessary to make intricate interconnections of relay contacts and switches. Examples of these circuits occur in automatic telephone exchanges, industrial motor control equipment and in almost any circuits designed to perform complex operations automatically.

But the topic was not completely new either. The study of the capacity to transmit telegraph signals was studied before Shannon. Compare:

  • Verdu, S. (1998). Fifty years of Shannon theory. IEEE Transactions on information theory, 44(6), 2057-2078.

I.e. Shannon is aware that switching electronic is used in various application domains and with increasing complexity. His thesis develops a theory for this situation. Today we have massively complex and scaled switching networks, which we call computers and post-hoc we look at Shannon through this lens. In fact, even his famous:

  • Shannon, C. E. (1948). A mathematical theory of communication. The Bell system technical journal, 27(3), 379-423.

When discussing information theory it is very much in the frame of a communication channel being disturbed by noise, and clearly a physical situation such as a telephone wire, or a wireless transmission situation is meant, but awareness of computing was present. Tukey would have already named the bit (see Shannon's remark on p. 1) and it being directly associated with a flip-flop circuitry. Shannon says:

This case has applications not only in communication theory, but also in the theory of computing machines, the design of telephone exchanges and other fields.

So by 1948, Shannon already merges the topics of digital communication and digital computing, post the appearance of the first working prototypes of computers.

What then is the first use of vacuum tubes for digital computation? Copeland gives Flowers (1934) credit for performing the first digital processing using vacuum tubes. It's in the context of controlling switching of telephone exchanges.

This again shows that one should think of communication technology such as telegraphy and telephony as important for leading into modern computing. Even the silicone revolution and the transistor would not change this. Analog tube radios became analog transistor radios but the understanding of the use of either for amplification and switching remained, hence silicon based computing was very much relatable to vacuum tube flip-flops.

query:
What was the first international scientific conference?

I tried to find which was the first large scientific conference but I could not find much. Bigg et al. The art of gathering: histories of international scientific conferences (2023) does not cite other conferences aside from the first Solvay conference (1911). The 1860 Karlsruhe Congress and the 1853 International Statistics Congress are only found in footnotes. It fails to give precise examples in the main text and does not say which could have been the first. I think that before the establishment of international conferences, scientist just gathered in their respective national science academy. What are the first examples of international gatherings of scientists?
gold_answers:
The same source I added says that there was a conference in 1798. I could not verify it but I think is this one:

  • Congress on Definitive Metric Standards, 1798-1799

The introduction fits the bill:

I have asked several historians of science what they consider to have been the first international scientific conference. A common answer is the Karlsruhe Congress of 1860, which was concerned with chemical notation and atomic weights. Seven years earlier, the Belgian mathematician A. Quetelet convened the first International Congress of Statistics in Brussels. Earlier still, there was the Gesellschaft deutscher Naturforscher und Arzte, founded by Oken in 1822, although this was a national rather than an international organization.' Few historians of science seem to be aware of the international conference on the metric system, held in Paris in the midst of the Revolutionary Wars in 1798-1799. The fact that neither Great Britain nor the United States was represented has probably tended to conceal the existence of this meeting from English speaking historians, and continental historians have ignored it.

From M. Crosland, "The Congress on Definitive Metric Standards, 1798-1799: The First International Scientific Conference?", Isis 60, (1969).

I leave the question open if you have more examples.

I have been communicated another conference in 1798. If you think metrological conventions do not count there was an international congress of astronomy at Gotha in August 1798, one month after the Congress on Definitive Standards:

  • Seeberg Observatory, Germany - Unesco

query:
Why radioactivity and its lethal effects took so long to be discovered?

Why was radioactivity discovered by Henri Becquerel in 1886 and was not discovered before? We know of the existence of uranium since at least a century before that when it was isolated.

According to J. Emsley, Nature's building blocks : an A-Z guide to the elements (2003)

In the late Middle Ages, the mineral pitchblende (uranium oxide, U3O8) often turned up in the silver mines of Joachimsthal (now part of the Czech Republic, but then part of the kingdom of Bohemia) and was thought to contain zinc or iron, but it was of little use.

He also adds:

For most of the nineteenth century, uranium was not regarded as particularly dangerous and commercial uses were found for it. For example, in 1855 a factory was set up in Austria to manufacture uranium pigments for colouring pottery and glass. Glass to which uranium oxide had been added had a fluorescent yellow-green colour.

If we had access from such a long time, why don't we have some accounts of uranium ores or any other radioactive material having unusual properties or being lethal before its discovery? Did glass makers die of unusual causes? Maybe somebody considered that it was at least toxic before the end of the 19th century.
gold_answers:
Pitchblende isn't very radioactive. Typical activity is on the order of 150 kBq/g, mostly in the form of alpha radiation. Hold a 1-kg chunk in your hand for an hour, and you'll absorb about 20 milliSieverts of radiation. For comparison, that's five times the typical yearly background dose, or one-fifth of the radiation needed to raise your lifetime risk of cancer by 1%.

Inhaling powdered pitchblende is certainly hazardous to one's health, but so is inhaling non-radioactive powdered quartz. From a medical standpoint, there's no signature symptom that makes a pitchblende miner dying of chronic radiation poisoning stand out from a hard-rock miner dying of silicosis or a coal miner dying of black lung.

This means that any discovery of radioactivity needs to come from scientific analysis. Historically, that happened when photographic plates were exposed to uranium salts (not possible before the 1839 development of the daguerrotype process). In theory, radioactivity could have been discovered from scintillation, but most natural scintillators are insensitive to the alpha radiation produced by common radioactive materials.

Historically, the dangers of high-dose radiation weren't discovered until X-rays provided a way of exposing things to intense radiation. Even then, it took about a decade to solidly establish that the X-rays themselves were harmful, as early methods of generation also produced known hazards such as ozone and ultraviolet light.

The effects of low-dose radiation are probabilistic, unlike the clear cause-and-effect of high-dose radiation. Discovering them required the development of statistical techniques for analyzing population-scale datasets, and the data-handling technology to gather that data, both of which happened in the 1930s and 1940s.

query:
How do we know that Newton and Leibniz discovered calculus independently?

  1. How do we know that Newton and Leibniz discovered calculus independently, or is it just a community agreement that both get the same credit? If Leibniz published calculus first, do we have papers on Newton's calculus before that date? Why did Newton accuse Leibniz, how could he see his papers (at his home) if he didn't publish anything?

  2. What is the probability that two men discover the same math at the same time?
gold_answers:
There is an enormous literature on this, and the story is known in great detail. And this literature is easily accessible. In the very abbreviated form it is the following. Newton did not publish his discoveries in Calculus when he made them, but we know about them from his manuscripts and correspondence. His correspondence with Leibniz contains some hints and coded sentences. On the other hand Leibniz published his discoveries as soon as he made them. By the way, his version of calculus had a very different form from Newton's.

Many years later, Newton and his followers started the priority fight. By the time of this fight, Leibniz's calculus was already widely used. There is no doubt that Newton discovered Calculus somewhat before Leibniz, but the discovery of Leibniz was independent, and the form in which Calculus is used nowadays is due to Leibniz, not Newton.

This unfortunate priority dispute led to a long stagnation in British mathematics, because Newton's followers refused to use the more advanced form of Calculus discovered by Leibniz.

query:
How and when did the extensionality principle for sets become so canonical?

Zermelo had the Axiom of Extensionality in his 1908 article which was translated to Investigations in the foundations of set theory I in Jean van Heijenoorts collection From Frege to Gödel: A Source Book in Mathematical Logic, pp. 199-215.

Expressions to the effect that the extensionality principle is constitutive for the very meaning of the notion of set are often seen in writing.

But in some modern accounts such as

Gandy, R. (1959). On the Axiom of Extensionality II. J. Symb. Log. 24.4, pp. 287–300.

and

Scott, D. (1962). More on the Axiom of Extensionality. Essays on the Foundations of Mathematics. Ed. by Y. Bar-Hillel et al. 1st ed. Amsterdam: North Holland.

and

Friedman, H. (1973). The Consistency of Classical Set Theory Relative to a Set Theory with Intuitionistic Logic. J. Symb. Log. 38.2, pp. 315–319.

the axiom of extensionality is not presupposed in the theories presupposed for their relative consistency proofs.

Such results as obtained by Friedman, Gandy, and Scott suggest that it could be useful to take non-extensional set theories as more fundamental, as they have more interpretations.

1 Does the extensionality principle have a lore which goes back to literature before the cited paper by Zermelo?

2 Are there specific contributions in the mathematical or philosophical literature which in interesting ways bolstered the canonicity of the extensionality principle?

Edit: As regards 2,

Maddy, Penelope (1988). Believing the Axioms. I. Journal of Symbolic Logic 53.2, pp. 481–511. doi: 10.2307/2274520.

gives a succinct but informative account on considerations regarding the Axiom of Extensionality on pages 483-484:

"Extensionality appeared in Zermelo's list without comment, and before that in Dedekind's [1888, p. 451. Of all the axioms, it seems the most "definitional" in character; it distinguishes sets from intensional entities like properties or concepts. Most writers seem to echo the opinion of Boolos [1971,p. 5011, that if any sense can be made of the distinction between analytic and synthetic, then the Axiom of Extensionality should be counted as analytic. (See also Shoenfield [1977, p. 3251, and Wang [1974, p. 5331.)

Fraenkel, Bar-Hillel and Levy give a bit more in their [1973, pp. 28, 871. query:
Did Jacques Charles first attempt to use the Celsius scale in his gas law?

In the late 1700's, Jacques Charles discovered the relationship between volume and temperature in gases keeping pressure constant. He used the Kelvin scale; however, the Kelvin scale was not developed by William Thompson ( Lord Kelvin) until 1848. gold_answers:
Short description: There is no evidence that Jacques Charles ever used Celsius or kelvins for his experiment, the Kelvin scale was invented much later.

Charles performed some experiments but did no publish them. Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac published a work on the dilation of gases in 1802. He compiled several experiments in the second section (Article 2), including Charles'. He leaves Charles' experiment for last, stating (p.. 157)

Avant d'aller plus loin, je dois prévenir que quoique j'eusse reconnu un grand nombre de fois que les gaz oxigène, azote, hydrogène et acide carbonique, et l'air atmosphérique se dilatent également depuis 0° jusqu'a 80°, le cit. Charles avait remarqué depuis 15 ans la même propriété dans ces gaz; mais n'ayant jamais publié ses résultats, ce par le plus grand hasard que je les ai connus.

[Google translation:] Before going further, I must warn that although I had recognized a great number of times that the gases oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen and carbonic acid, and atmospheric air expand equally from 0° to 80°, the cit. Charles had noticed for 15 years the same property in these gases; but having never published his results, it was by the greatest chance that I was made aware of them.

Then, Gay-Lussac explains Charles' experiment stating

Le gaz qu'il voulait mettre dans l'expérience était renfermé dans le reservoir d'un baromètre à la temperature 0°, sous la pression de 28 pouces de mercure.

[Google translation:] The gas he wanted to put into the experiment was enclosed in the reservoir of a barometer at a temperature of 0°, under a pressure of 28 inches of mercury.

Throughout the document Gay-Lussac refers to 0° as the temperature of frozen water. However, throughout the section (Article 2) the scale used in the experiments is divided in 80 divisions up to boiling water which means that they were using the Réaumur scale. The centigrade scale (Celsius) was formalized over the Réaumur scale in 1794 in France. This convention happened after Charles' experiment. Gay-Lussac in Article 4 when reporting his results, he reports using both in thermometer scale with 80 divisions (Réaumur) and another scale with 100 divisions (Celsius).

Gay-Lussac does not extrapolate his laws below 0°C, stating that for very low temperatures gases liquify. So he did not conclude anything about absolute 0 temperature. For earlier scientists that did attempt to project their scale down, see this entry from Encyclopedia Brittanica 1911 "Cold".

query:
Origin of module theory

A mathematician named Emmy Noether developed module theory, which is a theory that extends from ring theory. Module theory is widely used in mathematics, but it has become an essential theory in mathematical research to the point that it is also used in physics. That's why I became interested in module theory. What was the motivation or historical background that led Emmy Noether to create module theory? And additionally, what is the etymology of the word module in module theory, and why was it named that way?
gold_answers:
Emmy Noether introduced the modern abstract concept, but the theory of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, along with the term, is due to Dedekind in 1871, see Gray, A History of Abstract Algebra, 17.4 and MathOverflow thread. Noether's theory was an abstract generalization of Dedekind's, part of her general program of detaching algebra from concrete realizations like numbers and polynomials.

Dedekind's motivation was his studies of factorization of algebraic integers along the lines introduced earlier by Kummer to prove Fermat’s Last Theorem in special cases. Ideals first came up in the same work. The word "module" was Dedekind's self-translation of German Modul into French in his Sur la Théorie des Nombres entiers algébriques (1877). E.T. Bell then transplanted it into English in Successive Generalizations in the Theory of Numbers (1927). According to Stillwell, who translated Dedekind's Theory of Algebraic Integers into English, "Dedekind presumably chose the name 'module' because a module $M$ is something for which 'congruence modulo $M$' is meaningful."

From Gray:

"Dedekind turned to build up his general theory. He called a module a system (i.e., in later language a set) a of numbers closed under addition and subtraction. (It is indeed a $\mathbb{Z}$ module in modern terminology.) He said that if the difference of two numbers belonged to $\mathbf{a}$ then they were congruent modulo $\mathbf{a}$, written $ω ≡ ω'\pmod{\mathbf{a}}$.

He then said that if all the members of a module $\mathbf{a}$ are members of a module $\mathbf{b}$ then a is a multiple of $\mathbf{b}$ and that $\mathbf{b}$ divides $\mathbf{a}$. To remember this, note that $6$ is a multiple of $3$ and the set of multiples of $6$ is a subset of the multiples of $3$. The set of elements common to $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ he called the least common multiple of the two modules. He called the set of all sums of the form $α+β$, where $α$ is in $\mathbf{a}$ and $β$ is in $\mathbf{b}$, the greatest common divisor of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. He then introduced the concept of an ideal in a number field... The algebra of modules extends to ideals."
